examples.answer: When training and held-out errors are both high I suspect insufficient capacity. If training looks good but validation is bad I suspect sensitivity to the sample. Plot both errors as we add examples. A larger model can address underfitting; more examples or stronger regularisation can address overfitting.
A model that memorizes training examples but fails on the holdout has high variance. I would gather more examples or regularize it.
High bias means excellent training accuracy and poor validation accuracy. More capacity always fixes variance. Learning curves are unnecessary.

Lasso adds the absolute sizes of the coefficients to the loss, so some become exactly zero. Ridge uses their squares, spreading weight across correlated inputs. Lasso may keep an arbitrary member of a correlated group. Elastic net mixes both penalties for sparse but more stable selection.
L1 uses absolute coefficient magnitudes and can eliminate features. L2 uses squared coefficient magnitudes and tends to retain correlated predictors together.
Both penalties always set every correlated coefficient to zero. ElasticNet is a neural network architecture.

Among cases assigned an eighty percent probability, about eighty percent should occur. That matters when a payment decision depends on expected loss. I would inspect a reliability plot and Brier score, then learn an isotonic or Platt mapping on held-out validation data. Excellent discrimination does not guarantee trustworthy probabilities.
A model is calibrated if predicted probabilities agree with observed frequencies. This matters when thresholds use financial costs.
Calibration is just sorting examples correctly. A high AUC guarantees calibrated probabilities. Fit the calibrator on the test labels before reporting results.

During fitting, independently drop some activations at random. This discourages features from depending too much on particular partners. With inverted dropout, multiply the survivors by one over the keep probability during training. At ordinary prediction time all units are enabled and no dropout mask is sampled.
During training we randomly mask activations. For normal inference dropout is turned off.
Keep dropout enabled for every ordinary prediction and never scale activations. It drops the least useful neurons permanently.

Assuming independent zero-mean unit-variance query and key entries, adding d products gives a dot product with variance d. Those large logits push the softmax toward saturated probabilities and tiny derivatives. Rescale by the square root of the key width to keep variance near one and gradients usable.
Large attention scores saturate softmax. Dividing scores by the square root of the key dimension stabilizes their variance.
We multiply by the key dimension to make softmax as saturated as possible. Larger logits always improve gradients.

BERT is an encoder whose tokens can use both left and right context, trained to recover masked tokens. GPT predicts the next token with an attention mask that hides future tokens. BERT representations suit classification and other understanding tasks, while a causal decoder produces text one token at a time.
BERT reads context on both sides and learns to recover hidden words.
BERT and GPT both see future target tokens during generation. BERT has no masking objective and GPT predicts randomly masked words.

Covariate drift means the distribution of inputs changes; concept drift means the mapping from inputs to labels changes. Without labels I can watch feature distributions and proxies, but a shift alone does not establish that accuracy fell. When delayed outcomes arrive I measure performance on those cohorts.
Data drift is a change in the input distribution. Concept drift changes the conditional distribution of the target given inputs.
Any change in feature distribution proves the model is wrong. Delayed labels are irrelevant because drift detectors measure accuracy directly.

Run a shadow model on copied traffic without letting it decide user outcomes. A canary handles a small portion of live decisions. Blue-green keeps two prepared environments and switches traffic between them. Before any release agree on guardrail metrics and how to revert.
Shadowing means evaluating copied traffic without affecting the user. A canary takes a small fraction of actual user requests.
Shadow deployment immediately replaces all live decisions. A canary is an offline training dataset. No rollback is needed if offline accuracy is high.

Precision divides true positives by predicted positives, TP plus FP. Recall divides true positives by actual positives, TP plus FN. F1 is twice precision times recall divided by their sum. Explicitly return a documented value when the denominator is zero. Test perfect classifications, no actual positives and no positive predictions.
Precision is TP over TP plus FP, and recall is TP over TP plus FN.
Precision is TP over TP plus FN. Recall is TP over TP plus FP. F1 is their arithmetic mean. Division by zero cannot happen.

Parse documents into chunks and index each with owner and permission metadata. Filter retrieval by the caller permissions and recheck authorization on evidence before returning it. Use search and a reranker to select context. Cite the supporting passages and decline when evidence is missing. Evaluate retrieval separately from generation and refresh changed documents in the index.
Break documents into indexed chunks with ownership metadata. Combine retrieval with reranking to select useful context.
Index every document in a shared store without access metadata. Trust the prompt to hide unauthorized passages. Never abstain or cite evidence.
